claim: Rootless cones look like craters but have no connection to a magma chamber; they form when lava flows cross wet ground such as swamps or ponds and cause steam explosions. Example: around Lake Mývatn, Iceland. (NASA uses only the term "rootless cones"; "pseudocrater" is not in the NASA text.)
value: rootless cone: lava over wet ground; no magma chamber link
as_of: 11 Feb 2020 (NASA Image of the Day; Landsat 8 image of 26 Jul 2017)
source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'A Volcanic Potpourri' (Mývatn, Iceland)
page_or_section: paragraph on Hverfjall and rootless cones
note: Date of the NASA page was not printed in the saved text. The cone is made by erupted lava (magma at the surface elsewhere) interacting with water, so it is 'rootless', not 'non-volcanic'. Sources vary on 'pseudocrater' vs 'rootless cone' naming; NASA uses 'rootless cone' only. claim: USGS: geysers, fumaroles (also called solfataras) and hot springs are generally found in regions of young volcanic activity; surface water seeps down to hot rock around a magma reservoir (active or recently solidified but still hot), is heated and rises. These features are sometimes called "dying volcanoes" because they seem to represent the last stage of volcanic activity.
source: USGS, Volcanoes (GIP), 'Geysers, Fumaroles, and Hot Springs'
note: DISAGREEMENT: USGS treats these as products of volcanic heat (post-volcanic / secondary), not as 'pseudo'. Exam-prep notes (not used as sources) list them under 'pseudovolcanic'. The answer should say they are volcanic-heat features, and classify them as 'secondary' not 'false'. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: wording now matches USGS ("because they seem to represent"); earlier text stated it flatly. "Secondary" or "post-volcanic" is our classification, not a USGS term. Lines 370-381 verified.

claim: Fumaroles: openings through which a volcano releases gas even when not erupting; USGS (2008 text) says water vapour is the largest part of volcanic gas (it states more than 90%; see note). Hydrogen sulphide from fumaroles oxidises to sulphuric acid and native sulphur, colouring rocks.
source: USGS fact sheet 002-97 and GIP text

note: GEO-04 V005 records a CONFLICT on the 90% figure; use 'mostly water vapour'. Glossary copy saved as sources/usgs_of96-24_glossary.txt. claim: Baratang Island (Andaman) mud volcano: the Jarawa Creek vent has produced mud with illite and kaolinite, microfossils, volcanic glass, brine, methane gas and sulphide (pyrite) nodules, which are of sedimentary origin.
source: Achyuthan and Eastoe, J. Geological Society of India 53(3): 329-334 (abstract via US DOE OSTI)
note: Reuse of GEO-04 V049 evidence. The abstract also lists 'volcanic glass' in the ejecta, so the vent is not simply 'free of volcanic material'. No GSI or other official Indian page on Baratang was opened (see row 11).
